summary:
The Free State province of the Republic of South Africa stands under the national framework set by the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, which prohibits unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex, gender and sexual orientation. The Promotion of Equality and Prevention of Unfair Discrimination Act (PEPUDA) gives effect to that guarantee through the Equality Court. South Africa was the first country in the world to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, doing so in 1996, and the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 explicitly extends protection to gender identity and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation.

Partner status is recognised for a trans visitor travelling with a spouse. The Constitutional Court's judgment of December 2005 compelled Parliament to act, and the Civil Union Act was passed in November 2006 with a National Assembly vote of 229 to 41, legalising same-sex marriage nationwide.

Legal gender recognition is available under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act of 2003, which allows sex status to be changed in the population registry and therefore on identity documents and passports on proof of medical treatment such as hormone therapy, without requiring surgery. The Act demands medical evidence, a pathologising route that locks some people out of recognition altogether, and its binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; reform toward self-determination is pending but not in force. The cost of affirming one's gender through this process is described as dauntingly high. Where documents do not match presentation, trans people face humiliation, denial of service and threats of arrest for alleged fraud. A 2024 Gender Dynamix report records a trans woman who was met with police mockery and refused when she attempted to file a domestic-violence complaint after producing her identity document.

The ruling of the High Court of South Africa, Gauteng Local Division sitting as an Equality Court, in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (case 2024/070075, judgment 10 November 2025) is binding on the Department of Correctional Services nationwide. The court held that refusing a transgender inmate feminine attire, she/her pronouns and other gender expression, and refusing her prescribed gender-affirming hormone therapy, constituted unfair discrimination, and that hormone therapy forms part of the constitutional right to adequate medical treatment under section 35(2)(e). Orders were granted compelling the Department to provide hormone treatment at state expense, to permit clothing and cosmetics expressing the inmate's gender identity, to implement the accommodations required by its own standard operating procedure for transgender inmates, and to deliver prescribed medical care. The South African Human Rights Commission's National Preventive Mechanism, which holds the OPCAT monitoring mandate over places of deprivation of liberty, welcomed the judgment on 14 November 2025; the Department had argued that the therapy was cosmetic.

Detention nonetheless remains a site of elevated risk. The Department of Correctional Services already had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the ruling, and reporting of August 2025 recorded that rights organisations doubt whether it is implemented in practice.

Violence against trans people is documented and ongoing. On 26 December 2024 Aobakwe Mahlobo, a 23-year-old trans woman and make-up artist, survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a tavern in Tshwane that left her with severe facial injuries and lasting physical and emotional scars; she spoke out publicly and an arrest was reported. OUT LGBT Well-being's rights watch for December 2024 recorded five LGBTQIA+ murders that month, and violence disproportionately affects Black lesbian, trans and gender-nonconforming people in townships.

Access to gender-affirming care is uneven, and the pattern bears directly on Free State residents: treatment is concentrated in the main cities, so trans people in the province must travel long distances to reach it, private treatment costs hundreds of thousands of rands, and public waiting lists are long. Activists elsewhere in the country have delivered a memorandum to a provincial hospital over treatment delays running to a year. Academic analysis published in 2024 concludes that PEPUDA read with section 9 of the Constitution does not secure equal treatment for transgender and non-binary people in practice as regards gender-segregated bathrooms, so restroom and changing-room disputes remain foreseeable for visitors.
tangentialFactors:
The national protection machinery predates the current statute. The Justice Department's National Task Team, established in 2011, and the National Intervention Strategy for LGBTI Communities of 2014 were designed to coordinate responses to hate crimes against LGBT people, and sit alongside the Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act of 2024 rather than replacing them.

Document-related mistreatment is not confined to police encounters. The Gender Dynamix finding concerns a woman attempting to report domestic violence, indicating that a mismatch between identity documents and presentation can block access to protection services at the point of complaint, not only expose a person to arrest.

Care delays have been contested outside this province as well: activists in East London delivered a memorandum to Frere Hospital over gender-affirming treatment delays running to a year. The Free State's position differs in that residents must travel to the main cities to reach such care at all, rather than pressing a local facility for faster appointments.

The Mokoena judgment concerns a correctional facility, and its reach flows from national law rather than from any provincial authority; the orders bind the Department of Correctional Services across all facilities, as does the standard operating procedure the court ordered the Department to implement.
localsOnly:
Gender recognition reform toward self-determination is pending in the national legislature but is not in force, so residents continue to route through medical evidence and a binary classification under the 2003 Act until that changes.

Gender-affirming care is concentrated in the main cities. Free State residents therefore travel long distances for treatment, pay hundreds of thousands of rands privately if they can, or join long public waiting lists.

The Department of Correctional Services had a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners before the November 2025 judgment, and rights organisations questioned in August 2025 whether it is carried out in practice; the court's orders now require implementation and are enforceable through the Equality Court.

The Equality Court, established under PEPUDA, is the route through which residents bring claims of unfair discrimination on sex, gender or sexual orientation, including claims of the kind granted in the Mokoena case.
outOfScopeNotes:
Free State-specific trans sources were not surfaced in this inventory. The adjacent Free State reference produced no usable finding, so the assessment rests on the national framework and on the province's documented position regarding travel for care. Free State-specific data on hate-crime reports, Equality Court outcomes, policing practice and public-hospital waiting times remains unsourced here.

The sources disagree on the date of the Mokoena judgment: the court record gives 10 November 2025, while the parent-framework text states 14 November 2025, which is the date of the South African Human Rights Commission's media statement welcoming the ruling. The discrepancy is unresolved.

The 2024 academic analysis of bathroom access is scholarly conclusion rather than a holding of a court, and no reported judgment squarely deciding facility access for trans people was located in this inventory.

The status of pending gender-recognition reform, including any draft bill and its timetable, is described generally in the sources and is not sourced to a specific legislative instrument here.
